input: Turning to staffing, it is important to note that a significant gap has emerged in the commissioning programme. Two of the engineers who were assigned to the commissioning team have unfortunately been reassigned to support the turnaround, and their replacements will not be available until the turnaround has been completed. As a result, a staffing gap of 7 weeks has opened up in the commissioning programme, affecting in particular the loop-checking activities and the pre-start-up reviews that are required before mechanical completion can be declared. It should be noted that other activities, including document control and the clearance of the EPC contractor's punch list, are continuing in line with the plan, so the impact is limited to the work packages that the reassigned engineers were due to lead. In order to mitigate this issue, it is proposed that the commissioning packages be resequenced, so that the systems that are unaffected by the turnaround are dealt with first and the systems that depend on the turnaround are moved to the end of the programme. The project board will take ownership of this mitigation, approving the revised programme and monitoring progress against it at each status meeting. While this approach does not eliminate the gap entirely, it helps to ensure that the exposed work is moved to a point at which the replacement engineers will be available, thereby reducing the overall risk to the completion date.
target:
Commissioning carries the gap. Two of the engineers assigned to the commissioning team have been reassigned to the turnaround, and their replacements cannot be released from operations until the turnaround closes, which leaves a staffing gap of 7 weeks in the commissioning programme. The gap falls on the loop-checking and pre-start-up review work, both of which sit on the path to mechanical completion. Work that does not depend on the commissioning team — document control, training material, the EPC contractor's own punch-list clearance — continues at the planned rate, and the gap is confined to the tasks the reassigned engineers were to lead. Mechanical completion holds its date only if the resequenced order below is accepted by operations, whose permits govern access to the systems concerned.

The mitigation is a resequencing of the commissioning packages so that systems not affected by the turnaround are checked first and the turnaround-dependent systems move to the end of the programme. The project board owns the mitigation: the board approves the resequenced programme and reviews progress against it at each status meeting. Resequencing does not remove the gap; it moves the exposed work to the point where the replacements are available, and the recovery depends on the turnaround closing on its planned date. The alternative of leaving the programme order unchanged was set aside: it concentrates the whole gap at the end of commissioning, where no float remains. A slip in the turnaround extends the gap week for week, and the board's review is the point at which a further measure — contract commissioning support, at a cost not yet priced — would have to be authorised.
